title: Nepal’s parliament debates capital punishment following rape and murder of a three-year-old - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s parliament debates capital punishment following rape and murder of a three-year-old  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The rape and subsequent murder of a three-year-old girl in Jeetpur-Simara Sub-Metropolitan City of Bara district last week dominated the House of Representatives meeting on Monday, with lawmakers questioning whether existing laws and state institutions have done enough to protect women and children.

Some lawmakers, including ones from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party, even called for a constitutional amendment to Article 16(2) to permit capital punishment for heinous crimes, arguing that Nepal’s circumstances had changed since it committed itself to international instruments seeking abolition of the death penalty.

However, Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Sobita Gautam and Home Minister Sudan Gurung ruled out capital punishment, saying the government cannot introduce it without amending the constitution.

“Article 16(2) of the constitution explicitly prohibits the enactment of laws that impose capital punishment,” Gautam said. “Nepal is also bound by various international human rights treaties and instruments. Regardless of the intensity of public outrage, the government cannot legislate beyond the constitution.”

Nepal abolished capital punishment through the 1990 constitution, and the provision was retained in the 2015’s Constitution of Nepal. The country’s existing law already provides the maximum punishment available under the constitution for rape followed by murder. Section 41(f) of the National Penal (Code) Act 2017 provides for life imprisonment for murder committed after rape.

The debate on legal reform surrounding sexual violence intensified after five ministers signed a three-point agreement with the victim’s family on Saturday, committing to review existing laws and recommend changes aimed at introducing stricter punishment and speeding up justice in cases of sexual violence.

The agreement was signed by Home Minister Gurung, Law Minister Gautam, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal, Minister for Women, Children, Gender and Social Security Sita Badi, and Agriculture, Forestry and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary.

At the centre of the agreement is the formation of a seven-member ‘Garima Nyaya Sankalpa Samiti’ under the law ministry. The committee has been given seven days to submit recommendations on legal amendments concerning sexual violence, offences against women and children, and their penalties.

Previously, a task force led by Law Secretary Parashwor Dhungana had recommended changes to address obstacles in prosecuting rape and murder cases.

Among its recommendations were a review of the statute of limitations for filing rape complaints, continuous fast-track hearings for such cases and the classification of all sexual offences as crimes involving moral turpitude.

“Its draft recommendations will be combined with those produced by the new seven-member committee before being incorporated into a bill to amend the relevant laws,” Minister Gautam said.

She also cautioned against allowing public anger to determine the outcome of criminal cases, particularly while investigations are under way.

“The true test of the rule of law occurs precisely when public emotion is at its peak,” she said. “Prejudging cases before police investigations conclude, disseminating unverified information, interpreting evidence on social media and attempting to deliver a trial by public opinion weakens the administration of justice.”

Man Bahadur Aryal, joint secretary at the law ministry who represented the ministry in the earlier task force, said the review was not focused only on punishment.

“It examined procedural bottlenecks in criminal investigations, forensic processing and judicial adjudication,” Aryal said.

Legal experts say any reform should address the entire justice chain, from the police response and evidence collection to prosecution, trial and rehabilitation of victims.

Senior advocate Gopal Krishna Ghimire said Nepal’s laws already provide severe punishment for rape followed by murder, but weaknesses in investigation and delays in court proceedings often undermine justice.

“Victims of sexual violence face immense hurdles in securing timely justice, often compounded by weak police investigations,” Ghimire said. “Reform should focus on fast-tracking cases and ensuring robust evidence collection so that the guilty cannot escape while maintaining safeguards against wrongful prosecution.”

Under Section 219 of the National Penal (Code) Act, rape carries different penalties depending primarily on the age of the victim and the circumstances of the offence. Rape of a child below 10 years is punishable by life imprisonment.

The law defines life imprisonment in general terms as 25 years, while Section 41 provides for imprisonment for the remainder of the offender’s natural life for certain particularly serious offences, including murder following rape.

Deputy attorney general Sanjeev Raj Regmi said the legal framework already provides the highest punishment possible under Nepal’s constitutional system.

“Our legal framework already prescribes the absolute maximum penalty short of execution,” Regmi said. “Because the Constitution prohibits capital punishment, life imprisonment until death represents the highest statutory sentence available under Nepalese law.”

The bigger challenge, he said, is ensuring effective implementation.

Although existing procedures allow courts to hold continuous hearings in sensitive cases, fast-track provisions have not been consistently implemented across district courts.

The government’s seven-day deadline for the new committee now puts the focus on whether the proposed reforms will go beyond stronger language on punishment and address the long-standing weaknesses in investigation, forensic examination and judicial proceedings.

The demand for faster justice has long been part of Nepal’s debate on sexual violence. Although the law permits courts to conduct continuous hearings in sensitive cases, such provisions have not been implemented consistently across district courts.

The existing criminal justice process involves several stages. Police investigate the offence and submit their findings to the district government attorney’s office. Government attorneys then decide whether to file a charge sheet at the district court and prosecute the case on behalf of the state.

Delays can occur at multiple points, including investigation, forensic examination, preparation of the prosecution case and court proceedings.

Forensic evidence can be particularly important in sexual violence cases, but investigators have faced limitations in collecting, preserving and analysing evidence. Legal experts say stronger forensic capacity would reduce dependence on confessions and witness testimony and make prosecutions more robust.

The government has also discussed mechanisms for dedicated or continuous hearings in serious criminal cases. The law ministry and the Supreme Court have been working on ways to make fast-track proceedings more effective.

The legal reform process will ultimately determine whether the government can translate the public anger generated by the Bara case into reforms that strengthen investigation, prosecution and judicial proceedings while remaining within Nepal’s constitutional limits.

For victims and their families, however, the effectiveness of the reforms will be measured less by the severity of the law on paper than by whether the state can deliver timely, credible justice in practice.

title: Nepal's formalisation machinery is there: Now make it work - The Himalayan Times
description: Nepal's formalisation machinery is there: Now make it work  The Himalayan Times
publisher.title: The Himalayan Times
full_article:
Nepal does not suffer from a shortage of formalisation policy. What it needs now is a way of making the many institutions it has already built work together as one, and a clearer sense of what would make ordinary workers and small enterprises want to step into those systems on their own.

The scale of the challenge is worth stating precisely, because the numbers carry a lesson. The World Bank's recent analysis estimates that 81.8 percent of Nepal's employed working-age population was in the informal sector in 2023/24, well above global and regional averages. Nepal's last completed Labour Force Survey, from 2017/18, measured a narrower concept, informal-sector employment, at 62.2 percent.

Related Articles Nepal is not a prisoner of geography: A friendly note from across the Himalaya Health Ministry denies rabies vaccine shortage

The difference matters: the broader measure also captures some workers in otherwise formal enterprises whose employment lacks key protections, such as employer contributions to social security. Nepal's fourth Labour Force Survey is currently being conducted, and its eventual results will provide a much-needed update. Nepal's first National Economic Census, in 2018, found that nearly half of establishments operated without formal registration. A second Economic Census was conducted nationwide in 2026 and is expected to provide a far more current enterprise-level picture once its results are released.

Nepal has already built much of the machinery this next step requires. The Company Registrar's online platform is increasingly integrated with the tax authority, allowing a company's tax identification number to be generated through the registration process, proof that one government transaction can trigger another.

Customs tells a similar story: the World Trade Organisation's 2025 review found that 99.8 percent of Nepal's cross-border trade now operates under an interconnected digital system across major customs offices, alongside a national single window bringing government agencies together in one process. The National Planning Commission's current five-year plan names formalisation a structural priority, targeting basic social security coverage of 60 percent of the population by 2028/29, up from 32 percent.

Separately, 5.55 million tax identification numbers had been issued by fiscal year 2023/24. This year's budget also strengthened the incentive to participate in the formal system through preferential tax treatment tied to Social Security Fund contributions, a tangible reward for stepping into the formal economy.

Yet the Fund's own numbers show where the work remains. The International Labour Organisation (ILO) reported in late 2025 that nearly 2.7 million workers were registered with the Social Security Fund, but only about 1,500 informal and self-employed workers had enrolled. That gap, more than any single statistic in this piece, is where the next phase of formalisation must concentrate. Several municipalities have already begun using their own resources to extend coverage to informal workers, particularly women, proof that when formalisation is offered as something genuinely useful, people respond. Women are especially exposed to informality, particularly in agriculture and home-based work.

For a street/road-side shopkeeper, daily wage worker, construction worker, a vegetable seller, or a returning migrant, none of this is experienced as an architecture. It is experienced as forms, fees, and a simple question: what do I actually get in return? That question should shape the next phase, through flexible contribution options suited to seasonal and irregular income, and differentiated pathways for salaried workers, the self-employed, and migrants returning with skill and savings but no domestic contribution history.

The most promising fix is a shared architecture of identifiers, not one central database, linking enterprise, tax, worker, and social protection records so that recognition by one agency travels automatically to the next. Nepal's privacy law and emerging data-protection framework provide a starting point for building safeguards around such interoperability. Nepal should designate a coordinating authority with a mandate to set interoperability standards and publish an annual formalisation scorecard, so responsibility sits with someone rather than everyone's hope and no one's task. Local government also has a natural role, since business registration, market licensing, and social protection outreach all happen closest to citizens, at the municipal level, where national policy is either translated into real services or lost in translation.

Uruguay's Monotributo scheme offers a useful institutional lesson: by bundling tax compliance and social protection for small and self-employed workers, it treated formalisation as a single proposition rather than a series of obligations. Nepal need not copy Uruguay's institutions; it can copy the principle that citizens experience the state as one.

The ILO's renewed global push to implement Recommendation No. 204, its 2015 standard on transitioning from the informal to the formal economy, gives Nepal's own agenda a broader international framework, but the real test will be domestic implementation. Nepal's tripartite process has already produced a National Formalisation Action Plan, endorsed in 2022, and more recently an approved outline for a broader National Strategy on Formalisation. Nepal has also requested a three-year extension of its LDC graduation date, to 2029. The request remains under UN consideration, so the currently established graduation date remains November 24, 2026. Whichever date ultimately applies, the underlying need is the same: a more productive, better-protected domestic workforce.

Nepal has built the pieces. The next test is whether those pieces can become a system, and whether that system gives people a reason to enter it. When a worker or small enterprise becomes visible to the state, the state must become more useful to them in return. That is the visibility bargain. Nepal now has the institutions to make it real.

title: Chandra Nahar to be linked with tourism - The Rising Nepal
description: Chandra Nahar to be linked with tourism  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Aug. 25: Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Biraj Bhakta Shrestha has said the historic Chandra Nahar (Canal) in Saptari should be preserved as an important heritage site while being modernised to support agricultural production and promote tourism.

Inspecting energy and irrigation systems in Madhes Province, Minister Shrestha said the canal at Phattepur could be developed as a model linking irrigation, agriculture, heritage conservation and tourism.

He said the ministry was prepared to formulate plans in coordination with local governments for the protection, maintenance and rehabilitation of the century-old irrigation system. He also stressed that preserving the canal should be regarded as a shared responsibility of the government, local governments, water-user organisations and the wider community.

“Irrigation infrastructure does more than deliver water to farmland; it can make a multidimensional contribution to agricultural production, the local economy, employment and tourism,” Minister Shrestha said.

The Chandra Nahar, whose construction began during the reign of Chandra Shamsher, is known as Nepal's first modern state-built irrigation system.

This system, which brings water from the Triyuga River and provides irrigation facilities to about 10,500 hectares of agricultural land in Saptari, is an infrastructure built a century ago.

Minister Shrestha said it was no ordinary achievement that a structure built nearly a century ago was still delivering water to farmers’ fields, stressing the need to preserve its historical and technical significance and pass it on to future generations.

According to him, the ministry is seriously working on recommending the Chandra Nahar for inclusion in the World Heritage Irrigation Structures list of the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID).

“Nepal has a long and proud history of irrigation. It is the responsibility of our generation to preserve it, showcase its significance to the world and modernise it as necessary,” he said.

The Eastern Tarai Irrigation System Rehabilitation Project was implemented with grant assistance from the government of Japan to improve the deteriorating structures of the Chandra Nahar. Under the project, completed with a grant of around 2.25 billion Japanese Yen, 32 structures within the canal system were repaired and reconstructed.

The project involved the construction and improvement of eight canal underpasses, nine cross-drainage structures and 15 canal-crossing bridges.

Rehabilitation was undertaken after deteriorating structures had restricted water flow to around 80 per cent of the canal’s designed capacity, increased leakage and posed the risk of structural failure, according to the ministry.

Following rehabilitation, the project set a target of increasing the actual irrigated area from around 5,500 hectares to 10,500 hectares and raising the productivity of monsoon paddy from 3.65 tonnes per hectare to 4.38 tonnes per hectare.

The Chandra Nahar is also important to Saptari from the perspective of agricultural production and food security. As a major irrigation system based on a domestic water source—the Triyuga River—its sustainability is directly linked to agricultural production for thousands of farmers in the district.

Minister Shrestha said that regular maintenance was required from the main canal to its branch and distributary networks, and urged water-user organisations and local governments to play an active role in its preservation.

title: Lawmakers demand death penalty for rapists - The Himalayan Times
description: Lawmakers demand death penalty for rapists  The Himalayan Times
publisher.title: The Himalayan Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU, AUGUST 24

Members of Parliament from across the party lines in the House of Representatives today called for reforms in laws, including capital punishment for rapists after the rape and murder of three-year-old Garima Chaudhary in Bara.

Related Articles Three-year-old girl found dead in Bara; Police probe sexual assault Incessant Rain Studios, NIMB Ace Capital collaborate for Lost In Mandala

While acknowledging that capital punishment conflicts with constitutional guarantees and Nepal's international human rights commitments, lawmakers argued that Parliament must have the legislative strength to amend laws in response to severe public outrage.

The three-year-old went missing from her home in Dasdhure Tol, Jitpursimara Sub-Metropolitan City-1, on the morning of August 16. After her mother, Manmati Chaudhary searched for her unsuccessfully for over three hours, local police were alerted. Her body was recovered two days later in a nearby abandoned house.

Drawing on recent violent crimes against women in Nepal and elsewhere, several MPs urged the government to go beyond standard prison sentences and relief packages.

Prakash Pathak of the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) raised the murder of 25-year-old Lakshmi Rajbanshi, who was killed in her room in Japan, as well as the disappearance of 12-year-old Rebika Bishwakarma, a Grade VII student from Haldibari-2, Jhapa, who has been missing for two days.

Urging the Home Ministry to launch an immediate search for Bishwakarma, Pathak said: "Whether at home or abroad, our daughters are unsafe everywhere. Only those who endure it know the pain. Until when must our daughters become Lakshmi Rajbanshi, Nirmala Panta and Garima Chaudhary?"

Addressing constitutional limitations, Pathak added: "Sub-article 2 of Article 16 of the Constitution guarantees the right to live with dignity. But this does not mean protecting criminals and murderers ... Whether it is the constitutional restriction against enacting death penalty laws or human rights treaties to which Nepal is a state party, they must now be amended. This House must demonstrate that capability."

He proposed that convicted rapists and murderers should no longer receive standard state rations in prison and should instead face execution upon conviction.

Ashika Tamang, also of the RSP, called for extreme punishment: "If possible, provisions for hanging rapists must be made. If not, laws should be enacted to amputate the organ used to commit the rape."

Shraddha Kunwar Chhetri of RSP argued that punitive action should be determined by the severity of the crime rather than strict adherence to standard constitutional interpretation: "Pickpockets and rapists cannot be kept in the same room and punished equally."

Ranju Darshana of RSP noted the irony of daughters being unsafe in a society that reveres women, calling for awareness and reform initiatives beginning at the school level.

Shahjan Khatun and Ninukumari Karna of the Nepali Congress, Radhika Ramtel of the Shram Sanskriti Party, and Padma Aryal of the CPN-UML each questioned where perpetrators derive the audacity to commit such acts, calling on the state to strengthen control measures and provide formal answers.

Beyond calls for harsher punishment, several lawmakers sharply criticised the government's handling of the victim's family, rejecting administrative compromise agreements in favour of longterm justice.

Pramila Kumari Gachhadar of the Nepali Congress objected to the government's approach of reaching local administrative accords and offering relief packages: "I want to ask the government: Will erecting a statue bring back the life of a three-year-old girl? An agreement paper may temporarily stop protests, and relief may ease momentary pain, but it cannot restore long-term perception of justice and trust in the state."

She further demanded strict action against facilitators who attempt to broker compromises in cases of heinous crime, warning that senior ministers overriding local administration weakens public trust.

Balawati Sharma of the Nepal Communist Party (NCP) said the rape and murder of the child in Bara had brought shame upon the entire state and raised serious questions about executive accountability. "Daughters are unsafe in their own courtyards, creating a tragic situation where victim families must take to the streets to beg for justice," she said, urging the government to deliver immediate compensation to the family alongside strict justice.

title: Crisis deepens in Nepali Congress as 15th general convention nears - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Crisis deepens in Nepali Congress as 15th general convention nears  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, August 25

With the scheduled date for the Nepali Congress’ 15th General Convention drawing closer, the party has yet to resolve its political and legal disputes.

While one faction is waiting for the Supreme Court’s decision, another is calling for a political agreement to settle the dispute before the court ruling and create an environment for the general convention.

The Nepali Congress has scheduled ward-level conventions for September 9 as part of the 15th General Convention. However, the establishment-opposing faction has demanded that all convention activities be halted until the Supreme Court delivers its final verdict.

The faction has taken this position after the Supreme Court allowed a review of its earlier verdict in a case concerning the party’s official status.

Former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka said the Central Working Committee’s decision to move ahead with the 15th General Convention was against both the need for party unity and the Supreme Court’s decision to review the case.

“The decision recently taken by the Central Working Committee formed through the special general convention to move ahead with the 15th General Convention is clearly against both the historic need for complete party unity and the Supreme Court’s order to review the case,” he said.

Min Bishwakarma, coordinator of the publicity committee of the establishment-opposing faction, also said the convention process could not be unilaterally advanced while the case was sub-judice.

“When a case is pending in court, one side cannot naturally move the matter forward unilaterally,” he said. “But the process has been taken forward. Our side will file an application with the court on the matter.”

Little progress in dialogue

Although efforts are reportedly underway to resolve the dispute through dialogue, there has been little substantive communication between the leadership that emerged from the special general convention and the former leadership.

President Gagan Kumar Thapa has said he sought time for dialogue, but that it was not made available. Former president Sher Bahadur Deuba, meanwhile, appears to be waiting for the court’s final decision before engaging in discussions.

A conversation Deuba had with leaders who visited his Chundevi residence on Sunday also indicated his position on dialogue with Thapa. Nain Singh Mahar, who has recently taken on a mediating role, wrote on Facebook on Sunday that he had raised the need for a meeting between the two leaders.

“I also pointed out the need for a meeting and dialogue between President Gagan Kumar Thapa and him,” Mahar wrote. “He said he was making efforts to resolve the issue and suggested that we move forward after the court’s decision.”

The establishment faction expects former president Deuba to play a coordinating role in resolving the dispute.

General Secretary Pradip Paudel said efforts were being made to engage Deuba in dialogue and that the party was hopeful he would help with coordination.

“We are trying to meet and have a dialogue with the outgoing president. We are somewhat more hopeful about him,” Paudel told Onlinekhabar. “We expect that after meeting him, he will do something for coordination. We are also talking to others.”

Paudel stressed that the dispute should be resolved through political agreement rather than the courts.

“Our position is that we should resolve the party’s problems through mutual agreement and hold the convention at the scheduled time, rather than through the judicial process,” he said. “We will try to hold discussions and reach an agreement during the remaining 14 days.”

Paudel also said it was not appropriate for a political party to take its internal disputes to court.

“A party that advocates for the rule of law and the system of governance cannot naturally take its own internal problems to court,” he said.

Arguing that the party’s problems should ultimately be resolved through the general convention, Poudel said the establishment faction was ready to take any necessary steps to ensure a fair convention.

Nepali Congress leadership has recently appeared open to forming an organising committee to ensure the convention is conducted fairly.

Asked whether the party was prepared to form such a committee, Poudel said, “The leadership should be under the current president. We agree on everything else.”

‘A mechanism can be formed for management, not an organising committee’

Nepali Congress spokesperson Devraj Chalise said the party has no tradition of forming a general convention organising committee. However, he said a mechanism could be created for convention management and coordination.

“There is no provision for an organising committee in our party tradition. An organising committee will not be formed,” Chalise said. “But it can be given any name. The point is to seek advice and guidance from the leaders.”

He said any mechanism formed to facilitate an agreement would still have to operate within the party statute.

“If we use the provisions already in the statute, whatever name we give it, the issue ultimately concerns its role. We are ready to give that role,” he said. “Neither leaders nor cadres have the flexibility to amend or go beyond the statute.”

Chalise also said leaders and party workers who were left out during the membership update could be collectively included on the basis of a political agreement before the ward conventions begin.

‘General convention should be held under Deuba’s leadership’

The establishment-opposing faction has maintained that the 15th General Convention should be held under the leadership of former president Deuba as part of efforts to restore party unity.

The faction had also decided at a national gathering held in the final week of Shrawan to organise the convention under Deuba’s leadership.

NP Saud, a leader considered close to Deuba, said the current dispute should be resolved by using the 14th General Convention as the basis.

He said that because both sides had participated in the 14th General Convention, it should be recognised as the legitimate basis for moving ahead and creating an environment in which all sides could be included in the next convention.

“The case is before the court for review. Before it is settled, if an agreement is to be reached, both sides should be included since both participated in the 14th General Convention,” Saud told Onlinekhabar.

He also said holding the convention under Deuba’s leadership would provide a level playing field because the former president would not contest the upcoming election.

“Another important point is that Sher Bahadur Deuba, the president elected by the 14th General Convention, is not contesting himself,” Saud said. “Therefore, everyone gets an equal playing field. Everyone gets equal ground for competition.”

Saud said party unity could be achieved by recognising the leadership elected by the 14th General Convention. Otherwise, he said, the party would have to proceed according to the Supreme Court’s final decision on the party’s official status.

“The leadership elected by the 14th General Convention should be established. That will bring unity,” he said. “Otherwise, we will proceed according to whatever conclusion the review reaches.”

Three options proposed for unity

Nain Singh Mahar, who is leading the ‘Connecting Country and Congress’ campaign, believes the political leadership should take steps to resolve the dispute before the court delivers its decision.

He said he proposed three options to President Thapa during a recent meeting aimed at promoting party unity.

“I met Gagan in Gyaneshwar on the evening of the 20th. We spoke for around 25 minutes,” Mahar said. “I put forward three proposals to him.”

According to Mahar, Thapa expressed doubts about the possibility of reaching an agreement before the Supreme Court delivers its final decision.

“He kept saying, ‘What can happen before the court’s decision?’” Mahar said. “I told him it has to be done before the court’s decision.”

Mahar’s first proposal was to bring former president Deuba and President Thapa together for dialogue and resolve the party’s dispute.

“You two need to sit together. Whatever either of you has to give up, you should do it and unite the party,” Mahar said he told Thapa.

Mahar expressed optimism that direct dialogue between Deuba and Thapa could resolve the dispute.

“If the two of them sit together, they will reach an agreement. The dispute will be resolved,” he said.

His second proposal is to appoint a third person acceptable to both sides to oversee the general convention. His third is for both sides to publicly commit in advance to accepting the court’s decision and reach an agreement on the entire convention process.

“The second option is to give responsibility to a third person acceptable to both sides and hold the convention,” he said. “The third is to commit beforehand to accepting the court’s decision and reach an agreement on the entire convention process. That could also prevent a possible dispute after the court’s verdict.”

Mahar said the ‘Connecting Country and Congress’ campaign has continued discussions with various party leaders on party unity. He said he had also met former vice-president Purna Bahadur Khadka and leader Dr Shekhar Koirala to discuss the issue.

In Mahar’s view, the crisis in the Nepali Congress is linked less to a desire to split the party than to ego and mistrust among its leadership.

“No one appears to want the party to split. There is a little bit of an ego problem,” he said. “If a person or group works to reduce that ego problem, a solution can be found.”

He said the campaign was also engaging district presidents to build pressure from the grassroots for party unity.

Mahar stressed that the party should prioritise its institutional existence and future rather than who leads it.

“There is no alternative to uniting the party for the country and the people,” he said. “Even now, 99.9 percent of people want to see the party united. They want to see the party remain united.”

title: Nepali Congress MP Jagat Timilsina Questions Government's Foreign Policy and Diplomatic Practices - Ratopati
description: Nepali Congress MP Jagat Timilsina Questions Government's Foreign Policy and Diplomatic Practices  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Nepali Congress MP Jagat Timilsina has raised questions about the government's foreign policy and diplomatic practices.

Speaking during the zero hour in Tuesday's National Assembly meeting, MP Timilsina stated that the long-standing leadership vacuum in Nepal's foreign missions has affected Nepal's international reputation.

MP Timilsina argues that the absence of ambassadors in 21 out of Nepal's 31 embassies for a long time cannot be considered a mere administrative delay. 'An ambassador is not just an individual, but a representative of the state and national interest,' Timilsina said, 'The fact that important missions are run by acting heads for a long time is a question on Nepal's diplomatic capacity.'

Accusing the government of not being serious about foreign policy and representation, he emphasized that diplomacy must rise above traditional methods. 'In the changing global context, diplomacy should not be limited to formal meetings and banquets,' Timilsina added, 'The government should focus on attracting investment, technology transfer, expanding trade, and increasing Nepal's influence in international forums through digital and economic diplomacy.'

Questioning the government's working style, he urged that the diplomatic sector should not be limited to delays and formalities but should be linked to national interests. 'When will Nepal make an impact diplomatically?' he said, 'This issue, linked to national interest, cannot be delayed any further.'

title: 250 girls under 10 raped in Nepal in a year, most perpetrators known to victims - OnlineKhabar English News
description: 250 girls under 10 raped in Nepal in a year, most perpetrators known to victims  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
File image

Kathmandu

A total of 250 girls under the age of 10 were raped in Nepal on average each year over the past five fiscal years, according to Nepal Police data. Most cases reportedly involved perpetrators known to the victims.

A recent case in Bara has once again highlighted the vulnerability of young children. A three-year-old girl went missing from a squatter settlement in Jeetpur Simara Sub-Metropolitan City-1 on August 16. Her body was found two days later inside an abandoned house in Bhaktinagar.

Police arrested a 16-year-old boy in connection with the case after a trained sniffer dog helped investigators identify a suspect. Police said the teenager, who worked as a helper on a vehicle, confessed to raping and killing the girl after luring her with chocolate. The vehicle’s 24-year-old driver was also arrested.

According to Madhes Province Police chief DIG Om Adhikari, the accused teenager was acquainted with the victim. The girl frequently visited the driver’s house, where the teenager also went. Police believe the acquaintance was exploited to lure the child.

The Bara case is among several recent cases involving children. In Morang, a 31-year-old ward secretary was arrested and sent to prison on charges of raping a girl. In Rolpa, a teacher was arrested for allegedly raping a 12-year-old student after luring her to a secluded location.

Nepal Police data show that 268 girls under 10 were raped in fiscal year 2078/79 BS, followed by 259 in 2079/80 BS, 252 in 2080/81 BS, 217 in 2081/82 BS and 221 in 2082/83 BS.

Girls aged 11 to 16 constitute the largest group of rape victims. Police recorded 963 victims in this age group in fiscal year 2078/79 BS, 944 in 2079/80 BS, 1,009 in 2080/81 BS, 931 in 2081/82 BS and 966 in 2082/83 BS.

Overall, Nepal recorded 2,395 rape victims in fiscal year 2082/83 BS. Of them, 1,510 were girls under 18, while 885 were women aged 18 and above.

Police officials say most rape cases involving minors are committed by people known to the victims, including relatives, teachers, neighbours and acquaintances. Children are often lured through promises, gifts or other forms of persuasion.

Former DIG Hemant Malla said the pattern of perpetrators being known to victims is particularly common in cases involving minors.

Police have urged parents to remain vigilant about where their children go, whom they meet and changes in their behaviour.

The recent Bara case has also triggered calls for tougher punishment, including the death penalty. However, Nepal’s existing criminal law does not provide for capital punishment.

Under Section 219 of the National Penal Code Act, 2017, rape of a girl under 10, a person who is completely incapacitated or a woman above 70 carries life imprisonment. Rape of girls aged 10 to 14 carries 18 to 20 years in prison, while rape of girls aged 14 to 16 carries 12 to 14 years.

For victims aged 16 to 18, the punishment is 10 to 12 years in prison, while rape of women aged 18 and above carries seven to 10 years’ imprisonment.

The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl has sparked outrage across Nepal, with demands growing for a swift investigation and tougher laws.

The child went missing from her home in Bara, almost 127km from the capital Kathmandu in Madhesh province, on 16 August. Her mutilated and decomposed body was found at a nearby abandoned house three days later after neighbours reported a smell.

Police said a 24-year-old driver and a 17-year-old helper on a bus were among the suspects arrested in connection with the case.
